messages.body_plain:
Dear list users

I have a question puzzling me for a couple of weeks, so I am asking for your help on how to report my analysis.


I am using logistic regression to model 3 separate groups of participants' accuracy in a 192-trial task. The model is:
resp ~ ctrial * cnd + (1 + ctrial | sbj) + (1 | specific_stim)

with two types of responses (correct, wrong) regressed on a numerical predictor (trial is centered) and a factor (condition with 3 level: intensity, ideogram, pseudoword). There are 60 participants (20 in each condition), and specific_stim stands for the 16 stimuli I used (same in all condtions).


The ordering of the cnd factor is: int (intensity), ideo (ideogram), pseudo (pseudoword)

The results are:
Formula: resp ~ ctrial * cnd + (1 + ctrial | sbj) + (1 | specific_stim) 
   Data: train[train$day == "day3", ] 
   AIC   BIC logLik deviance
 12671 12744  -6325    12651
Random effects:
 Groups        Name        Variance   Std.Dev.  Corr   
 sbj          
 (Intercept) 8.8887e-01 0.9427988        
               ctrial      5.7517e-06 0.0023983 -0.046 
 specific_stim (Intercept) 1.3482e-01 0.3671834        
Number of obs: 11520, groups: sbj, 60; specific_stim, 16

Fixed effects:
                   Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)   
(Intercept)       0.4796092  0.2325019   2.063  0.03913 * 
ctrial            0.0022661  0.0008222   2.756  0.00585 **
cndideo           0.8783986  0.3044234   2.886  0.00391
 **
cndpseudo         0.8554317  0.3035756   2.818  0.00483 **
ctrial:cndideo    0.0010380  0.0012396   0.837  0.40237   
ctrial:cndpseudo -0.0015339  0.0012309  -1.246  0.21272   
---


So, if I am interpreting correctly, there seems to be no interaction of ctrial by condition, participants' accuracy is increasing as trials progress, and (since there is no interaction) participants in the pseudoword and ideogram conditions outperform participants in the intensity condition. Correct?

Then I need to compare participants' accuracy between the pseudoword and ideogram condition, so I re-leveled the cnd factor (pseudo, int, ideo), and re-run the model. 

The results are now a bit different:

Formula: resp ~ ctrial * cnd + (1 + ctrial | sbj) + (1 | specific_stim) 
   Data: train[train$day == "day3", ] 
   AIC   BIC logLik deviance
 12671 12744  -6325    12651
Random effects:
 Groups        Name        Variance   Std.Dev.  Corr   
 sbj           (Intercept) 8.8887e-01
 0.9427986        
               ctrial      5.7517e-06 0.0023983 -0.046 
 specific_stim (Intercept) 1.3482e-01 0.3671836        
Number of obs: 11520, groups: sbj, 60; specific_stim, 16

Fixed effects:
                 Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)     1.3350429  0.2344578   5.694 1.24e-08 ***
ctrial          0.0007337  0.0009157   0.801  0.42296    
cndint         -0.8554340  0.3035756  -2.818  0.00483 ** 
cndideo        
 0.0229662  0.3059054   0.075  0.94015    
ctrial:cndint   0.0015324  0.0012309   1.245  0.21316    
ctrial:cndideo  0.0025689  0.0013040   1.970  0.04883 *  
---


There is no effect of trial, and the interaction of ctrial :cndideo suggests that there is a significant difference in the rate of improvement between the pseudoword and ideogram groups. There is no such difference between the pseudoword and intensity groups (ctrial:cndint:  non-significant).

Correct me if I'm wrong: Although for ctrial = 0 (at the middle of the procedure) there seems to be no difference in accuracy between the pseudoword and ideogram groups (cndideo: non-significant), this doesn't stand for other values of ctrial (ctrial:cndideo: significant).
So, I recoded the trial predictor, so that 0 is set at the beginning or at the end of the procedure, and the results (not posted here) suggest that at these points (trial=0, trial=192) there is no difference in the odds of correct responding between the pseudoword and ideogram conditions. 


I also used plotLMER.fnc() to plot the interaction of trial by condition (please see the attached file).
The interaction plot suggests that 

(a) mean accuracy (or mean odds of correct responding) in the pseudoword and ideogram conditions is comparable. 

(b) the odds of correct responding increase as trials progress in the ideogram and intensity groups but not in the pseudoword group.


But, how do I report my results? 

(a) The critical comparison to test my hypothesis is the comparison between the pseudoword and ideogram conditions. Ho do I report that the odds of correct responding are comparable between the two conditions? 

(b) There is an effect of trial in the ideogram and intensity conditions, but not in the pseudoword condition. Do I have to split the data by condition and report these beta values, separately for each condition? Or do I report the beta values of the analysis of my pooled data (by setting the reference level at the appopriate condition)?

Thank you all for your time, and sorry for the long message.
I would greatly appreciate any reponse.

Sincerely,
Fotis A. Fotiadis

Dear Dr. Jaeger,

Thank you so much for your response.
I am following your suggestions, but I probably need a little quidance on contrast coding, since I am quite new with mixed logit models (treatment coding was used in my previous models, your guess was correct).

I've read the coding tutorial (http://hlplab.files.wordpress.com/2011/02/codingtutorial.pdf) I've found in your lab's blog (and I am also studing your 2008 JML paper). 

I've kept the ordering of my condition factor this way: intensity, ideogram, pseudowords because it is consistent with my hypothesis. I suppose it creates no problem.

I do not need to compare a condition with the mean of the other conditions, so I used the folling coding scheme (which I'm not sure it's Helmert coding, to be honest):

train$cnd_helm<-train$cnd

contrasts(train$cnd_helm)<-cbind("ideo_vs_int"=c(-0.5, 0.5, 0), "pseudo_vs_ideo"=c(0, -0.5, 0.5))


and then i run the model:

d3_contr<-lmer(resp~ctrial*cnd_helm + (1+ctrial|sbj)+(1|specific_stim), family=binomial, data=train[train$day=="day3",])


The results are:

So, is this the correct way to code my condition factor?

Now, about the assumption of linearity, I assume you are talking about a significant quadratic effect of ctrial, right?
I run the model: 

d3_contr_square<-lmer(resp~(ctrial+I(ctrial^2))*cnd_helm + (1+ctrial|sbj)+(1|specific_stim), family=binomial, data=train[train$day=="day3",])
in an effort to compare it with the first model, but there was a warning of false convergence. 

I am not sure how to test for a quadratic effect of trial (apart from the graphical inspection of my data which suggests linearity), since any attempt to simplify the model still led to false convergence. 


Thank you again for your time.
Fotis

Dear Fotis,

All the points aside that Florian alreadly addressed, part of your message
reflects a typical problem in interpreting the output of an lmer
in comparison with the output of an ANOVA. Since I ran into this problem
a couple of times when discussing the output of an lmer, it might
be worthwhile to highlight this here.

In fact, my post contains an answer to Fotis plus a question for the list.

You wrote:

> Fixed effects:
> ?????????????????? Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)??
> (Intercept)?????? 0.4796092? 0.2325019?? 2.063? 0.03913 *
> ctrial??????????? 0.0022661? 0.0008222?? 2.756? 0.00585 **
> cndideo?????????? 0.8783986? 0.3044234?? 2.886? 0.00391
>  **
> cndpseudo???????? 0.8554317? 0.3035756?? 2.818? 0.00483 **
> ctrial:cndideo??? 0.0010380? 0.0012396?? 0.837? 0.40237??
> ctrial:cndpseudo -0.0015339? 0.0012309? -1.246? 0.21272??
> ---
> 
> 
> So, if I am interpreting correctly, there seems to be no interaction of ctrial
> by condition, participants' accuracy is increasing as trials progress, and
> (since there is no interaction) participants in the pseudoword and ideogram
> conditions outperform participants in the intensity condition. Correct?

Actually, it is not correct. The correct test for an overall interaction is a model
comparison for a model with and without the interaction.
This might or might just not be significant in your case.

The thing is that the two regression weights for a 3x2 interaction (or the 3-level
factor with a covariate) are something different from an F-test in an AN(c)OVA.
The regression weights give you the differences for the "other" condition in
comparison to the one mapped onto the intercept. This means that the two 
conditions not mapped onto the intercept are not compared to each other.
An F test, however, takes into account the comparison of all conditions with each other.

If you look at the two regression weights for the interaction in detail,
it actually becomes obvious that a releveling may lead to a significant effect.

The simple (NOT main) effect for centered trial is clearly significant which 
means that performance gets better in the "intensity" condition mapped on the intercept
by 0.002261 per trial (as a side remark, it is easier to also normalize the range of the trial
numbers to -0.5 to 0.5, so that the regression weights shows you directly how much things
change over the course of the experiment).

This increase is larger (0.022 + 0.001, but not significantly so) in the "ideo" condition
and smaller (0.022 - 0.0015, again, not significantly so) in the "pseudoword" condition. 
This does mean, however, that there is the chance the increase may differ 
between the "ideo" and "pseudoword" condition (which indeed is what
your second analysis showed). In fact, if the standard errors are not too
different over the conditions, taking the difference in the z-value between
the two regression weights gives you a good first estimate for the difference
between the two condition (in this case 0.8 - (-1.2) = 2), which indeed
is close to the observed value. 

So, to sum things up, even with two non-significant regression weights
for an interaction in a 3x2 design, you cannot be sure that there is
no interaction, as the "middle" condition, which may be mapped on the intercept
may not differ from the "high" and the "low" condition,
while the latter two are significantly different.

And here comes my question:
Things actually get tricky when you have a three level factor. In most
cases, it is possible to get around multiple testing issues by a clever
choice of the intercept condition.

What to do if not? Is there any accepted multiple mean comparison procedure
for mixed-effect model (like Honest Significant Difference, of the Newman-Keuls
procedure for an ANOVA)? Obviously, one can relevel and apply Bonferroni, but
my understanding is that Bonferroni correction is a rather blunt instrument.

Kind regards,
Holger

As I understand your question, you're looking for an LME analogue of an "omnibus" ANOVA analysis (one which would give you an F-test where the numerator has more than one degree of freedom). In this situation I would suggest using a likelihood ratio test between models with and without a fixed effect the critical factor (or interaction of factors, as appropriate).  As long as your dataset is reasonably large in comparison to the number of parameters in your models, the likelihood-ratio test should be only minimally anti-conservative (in the same way that t-statistics in LME models for psycholinguistic datasets are generally pretty close to normally distributed) its result will be invariant to the parametrization (i.e. the contrasts) you choose to represent your factors, and it will give yo
 u a result that you can interpret in much the same way as you would have interpreted an omnibus ANOVA's results.

Best & hope this helps,

Roger

Dear Roger,

thanks for your reply. However, the test whether a factor
is significant or not via model comparison likelihood test
was clear to me.

The question is what to with multiple comparison, that is,
Let's say I have a factor with 4 levels, and there is a "main effect"
(i.e., the model with the three regression weights for the factor
is better than the model without). I now want to know which
means are significantly different from each other. To do that,
the only procedure that would give me all comparisons between
the four levels (A,B,C, and D)  is relevelling.

This procedure would like this:

The is my first model maps Level A on the intercept and I get the
comparisons
A vs B
A vs C
A vs D

then I map Level B on the intercept to get the comparisons
B vs C
B vs D

and finally I map C on the intercept to get
C vs D.

The significance treshold now would be 0.01666 (= 0.05/3).
First of all, I am not sure that this would actually be OK.
Seconsly, this is cumbersome and probably conservative. In the ANOVA paradigm,
I would be able to compute a Honest Significant Difference (HSD)
based on the MS(Error) which gives me a criterion for all comparisons
(e.g., if it would be an RT experiment, mean RTs would have to be 35 ms 
different from each other to be considered significantly different).

Kind regards,

Holger

Dear Holger, Fotis, et al.,

Just a quick point: I was recently pointed towards the 'multcomp'
package (esp. the function 'glht'), and this might be worth looking
at.  It provides a convenient way to examine arbitrary (i.e.,
user-specified) contrasts, also providing a correction algorithm for
multiple comparisons, which the authors claim (in a companion
published journal article) is general across a variety of methods (any
analysis which depends on a variance-covariance matrix), including
both regular lm(), glm(), and also, crucially, lmer() and glmer().

I can't admit to fully understanding the correction algorithm, but it
does produce results which are considerably less conservative than a
flat Bonferroni, so it's probably superior, and the paper's there if
you're interested in the details.  The first time I used it, it took
me a little time to understand exactly how to set up a contrast matrix
(hint: it's not the same as setting contrasts() in a factor), but it
works very nicely once you figure this out.

I'd recommend trying this out, both as a way to get
multiple-comparison corrections, and in place of re-leveling and
re-fitting a model to get different contrasts.  If you get stuck on
how to code the contrasts, let me know and I can give you some
pointers.

hope this helps,
-scott

For the problem of multiple pairwise comparisons that you're asking about, yes, it seems to me that releveling would be the right way to do things. I only have passing familiarity with Tukey's HSD for ANOVA, but let me ask a basic question about its application in mixed model ANOVA: if there are violations of sphericity, won't that be very bad for standard HSD computations, because they assume the same error term in the denominator for all pairwise tests?  (Of course, violations of sphericity are bad for mixed model ANOVA in general, but for the omnibus F statistic at least you're getting contribution from all the conditions to both the numerator and denominator.)

Roger

Dear Fotis,

All the points aside that Florian alreadly addressed, part of your message
reflects a typical problem in interpreting the output of an lmer
in comparison with the output of an ANOVA. Since I ran into this problem
a couple of times when discussing the output of an lmer, it might
be worthwhile to highlight this here.

In fact, my post contains an answer to Fotis plus a question for the list.

You wrote:

> Fixed effects:
> ?????????????????? Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)??
> (Intercept)?????? 0.4796092? 0.2325019?? 2.063? 0.03913 *
> ctrial??????????? 0.0022661? 0.0008222?? 2.756? 0.00585 **
> cndideo?????????? 0.8783986? 0.3044234?? 2.886? 0.00391
>  **
> cndpseudo???????? 0.8554317? 0.3035756?? 2.818? 0.00483 **
> ctrial:cndideo??? 0.0010380? 0.0012396?? 0.837? 0.40237??
> ctrial:cndpseudo -0.0015339? 0.0012309? -1.246? 0.21272??
> ---
> 
> 
> So, if I am interpreting correctly, there seems to be no interaction of ctrial
> by condition, participants' accuracy is increasing as trials progress, and
> (since there is no interaction) participants in the pseudoword and ideogram
> conditions outperform participants in the intensity condition. Correct?

Actually, it is not correct. The correct test for an overall interaction is a model
comparison for a model with and without the interaction.
This might or might just not be significant in your case.

The thing is that the two regression weights for a 3x2 interaction (or the 3-level
factor with a covariate) are something different from an F-test in an AN(c)OVA.
The regression weights give you the differences for the "other" condition in
comparison to the one mapped onto the intercept. This means that the two 
conditions not mapped onto the intercept are not compared to each other.
An F test, however, takes into account the comparison of all conditions with each other.

If you look at the two regression weights for the interaction in detail,
it actually becomes obvious that a releveling may lead to a significant effect.

The simple (NOT main) effect for centered trial is clearly significant which 
means that performance gets better in the "intensity" condition mapped on the intercept
by 0.002261 per trial (as a side remark, it is easier to also normalize the range of the trial
numbers to -0.5 to 0.5, so that the regression weights shows you directly how much things
change over the course of the experiment).

This increase is larger (0.022 + 0.001, but not significantly so) in the "ideo" condition
and smaller (0.022 - 0.0015, again, not significantly so) in the "pseudoword" condition. 
This does mean, however, that there is the chance the increase may differ 
between the "ideo" and "pseudoword" condition (which indeed is what
your second analysis showed). In fact, if the standard errors are not too
different over the conditions, taking the difference in the z-value between
the two regression weights gives you a good first estimate for the difference
between the two condition (in this case 0.8 - (-1.2) = 2), which indeed
is close to the observed value. 

So, to sum things up, even with two non-significant regression weights
for an interaction in a 3x2 design, you cannot be sure that there is
no interaction, as the "middle" condition, which may be mapped on the intercept
may not differ from the "high" and the "low" condition,
while the latter two are significantly different.

And here comes my question:
Things actually get tricky when you have a three level factor. In most
cases, it is possible to get around multiple testing issues by a clever
choice of the intercept condition.

What to do if not? Is there any accepted multiple mean comparison procedure
for mixed-effect model (like Honest Significant Difference, of the Newman-Keuls
procedure for an ANOVA)? Obviously, one can relevel and apply Bonferroni, but
my understanding is that Bonferroni correction is a rather blunt instrument.

Kind regards,
Holger

Hi Holger,

As I understand your question, you're looking for an LME analogue of an "omnibus" ANOVA analysis (one which would give you an F-test where the numerator has more than one degree of freedom). In this situation I would suggest using a likelihood ratio test between models with and without a fixed effect the critical factor (or interaction of factors, as appropriate).  As long as your dataset is reasonably large in comparison to the number of parameters in your models, the likelihood-ratio test should be only minimally anti-conservative (in the same way that t-statistics in LME models for psycholinguistic datasets are generally pretty close to normally distributed) its result will be invariant to the parametrization (i.e. the contrasts) you choose to represent your factors, and it will give you a result that you can interpret in much the same way as you would have interpreted an omnibus ANOVA's results.

Best & hope this helps,

Roger

Dear Holger, Fotis, et al.,

Just a quick point: I was recently pointed towards the 'multcomp'
package (esp. the function 'glht'), and this might be worth looking
at.  It provides a convenient way to examine arbitrary (i.e.,
user-specified) contrasts, also providing a correction algorithm for
multiple comparisons, which the authors claim (in a companion
published journal article) is general across a variety of methods (any
analysis which depends on a variance-covariance matrix), including
both regular lm(), glm(), and also, crucially, lmer() and glmer().

I can't admit to fully understanding the correction algorithm, but it
does produce results which are considerably less conservative than a
flat Bonferroni, so it's probably superior, and the paper's there if
you're interested in the details.  The first time I used it, it took
me a little time to understand exactly how to set up a contrast matrix
(hint: it's not the same as setting contrasts() in a factor), but it
works very nicely once you figure this out.

I'd recommend trying this out, both as a way to get
multiple-comparison corrections, and in place of re-leveling and
re-fitting a model to get different contrasts.  If you get stuck on
how to code the contrasts, let me know and I can give you some
pointers.

hope this helps,
-scott

I won't pretend that the following is the One True Way, but let's assume that:
(a) you'd like estimates and p-values for int vs. ideo, int vs.
pseudo, ideo vs. pseudo, and for the effect of trial (overall increase
in accuracy across the course of the experiment), and
(b) you wouldn't mind applying a reasonable correction for multiple comparisons

Try this (assuming your data's just called "train", and assuming the
levels of 'cnd' are int, ideo, and pseudo, in that order, as in your
example code):

###
library(lme4)
library(multcomp)

fit <- lmer(resp ~ ctrial + cnd + (1 + ctrial | sbj) + (1 |
specific_stim), family = "binomial", data = train)
contrast.matrix <- rbind( "Effect of Trial" =    c(0, 1, 0, 0),
                                    "Int vs. Ideo" =       c(0, 0, -1, 0),
                                    "Int vs. Pseudo" =   c(0, 0, 0, -1),
                                    "Ideo vs. Pseudo" = c(0, 0, 1, -1) )

summary(glht(fit, contrast.matrix))
###

For the matrix, the length of each vector is four, because you have
four linear effects in the model (intercept, ctrial, cndideo, and
cndpseudo).  The 1s are positioned to represent the linear combination
you're after. The first three are easy, since they all correspond
directly to the effects seen in the output of the model.  The only
slightly tricky one is the last, comparing ideo and pseudo. The way I
think about it is that the estimate of ideo is the "displacement" from
int, and the same with pseudo. So to compare the "displacement" of
ideo relative to pseudo, you just have the difference of their two
estimates.  Thus in the contrast vector, one is coded 1 and the other
is coded -1.  The signs throughout are just chosen to facilitate
interpretation. If you think of "int vs. ideo" as "how accurate is int
compared to ideo", then you expect a negative number (since int is
less accurate), so I put in a -1.  The interpretation of the final
contrast vector is "how accurate is ideo compared to pseudo?", and the
answer will be positive, but very small (0.886 minus 0.837).  If you
play around with re-leveling, you can confirm any of the contrast
choices you make, in case you're not sure you coded the contrast
matrix correctly.

The summary should give you all of the estimates at once, as well as
providing corrected p-values.  Again, I don't understand the math of
this particular correction in a deep way, but it seems reasonable
(i.e., less conservative than Bonferroni).  If you mistrust the
correction, you can just compute p-values directly from the z-values
provided, since those aren't adjusted.  But it's a convenient way to
get all your contrasts of interest at once, IMHO, even if you don't
use the correction.

best,
-scott

messages.subject: Collinearity among predictors and interaction
messages.body_plain:
Dear R-Lang-ers,

I'm running an lmer analysis over corpus data and am interested in whether the interaction between two variables, A:B is significant and if so, what the direction of the effect is.  

My model contains a number of predictors including cA, cB and cA:cB where cA is a binary categorical variable (coding: -1 and 1) and cB is a centered numerical variable (these 3 predictors are also entered as random effects).  The problem that I'm encountering is that the interaction term is collinear with cB, where the value from the correlation matrix is reported as -0.579.  I know that I can use model comparison to determine if the interaction is significant but the high collinearity makes me unsure about the size and direction of the beta weight.

Does anybody have any advice as to how to handle this situation?

Thanks!
Ariel

I won't pretend that the following is the One True Way, but let's assume that:
(a) you'd like estimates and p-values for int vs. ideo, int vs.
pseudo, ideo vs. pseudo, and for the effect of trial (overall increase
in accuracy across the course of the experiment), and
(b) you wouldn't mind applying a reasonable correction for multiple comparisons

Try this (assuming your data's just called "train", and assuming the
levels of 'cnd' are int, ideo, and pseudo, in that order, as in your
example code):

###
library(lme4)
library(multcomp)

fit <- lmer(resp ~ ctrial + cnd + (1 + ctrial | sbj) + (1 |
specific_stim), family = "binomial", data = train)
contrast.matrix <- rbind( "Effect of Trial" =    c(0, 1, 0, 0),
                                    "Int vs. Ideo" =       c(0, 0, -1, 0),
                                    "Int vs. Pseudo" =   c(0, 0, 0, -1),
                                    "Ideo vs. Pseudo" = c(0, 0, 1, -1) )

summary(glht(fit, contrast.matrix))
###

For the matrix, the length of each vector is four, because you have
four linear effects in the model (intercept, ctrial, cndideo, and
cndpseudo).  The 1s are positioned to represent the linear combination
you're after. The first three are easy, since they all correspond
directly to the effects seen in the output of the model.  The only
slightly tricky one is the last, comparing ideo and pseudo. The way I
think about it is that the estimate of ideo is the "displacement" from
int, and the same with pseudo. So to compare the "displacement" of
ideo relative to pseudo, you just have the difference of their two
estimates.  Thus in the contrast vector, one is coded 1 and the other
is coded -1.  The signs throughout are just chosen to facilitate
interpretation. If you think of "int vs. ideo" as "how accurate is int
compared to ideo", then you expect a negative number (since int is
less accurate), so I put in a -1.  The interpretation of the final
contrast vector is "how accurate is ideo compared to pseudo?", and the
answer will be positive, but very small (0.886 minus 0.837).  If you
play around with re-leveling, you can confirm any of the contrast
choices you make, in case you're not sure you coded the contrast
matrix correctly.

The summary should give you all of the estimates at once, as well as
providing corrected p-values.  Again, I don't understand the math of
this particular correction in a deep way, but it seems reasonable
(i.e., less conservative than Bonferroni).  If you mistrust the
correction, you can just compute p-values directly from the z-values
provided, since those aren't adjusted.  But it's a convenient way to
get all your contrasts of interest at once, IMHO, even if you don't
use the correction.

best,
-scott

> Actually, it is not correct. The correct test for an overall interaction is a model
> comparison for a model with and without the interaction.
> This might or might just not be significant in your case.
>
> The thing is that the two regression weights for a 3x2 interaction (or the 3-level
> factor with a covariate) are something different from an F-test in an AN(c)OVA.
> The regression weights give you the differences for the "other" condition in
> comparison to the one mapped onto the intercept. This means that the two
> conditions not mapped onto the intercept are not compared to each other.
> An F test, however, takes into account the comparison of all conditions with each other.
>
> If you look at the two regression weights for the interaction in detail,
> it actually becomes obvious that a releveling may lead to a significant effect.
>
> The simple (NOT main) effect for centered trial is clearly significant which
> means that performance gets better in the "intensity" condition mapped on the intercept
> by 0.002261 per trial (as a side remark, it is easier to also normalize the range of the trial
> numbers to -0.5 to 0.5, so that the regression weights shows you directly how much things
> change over the course of the experiment).

> This increase is larger (0.022 + 0.001, but not significantly so) in the "ideo" condition
> and smaller (0.022 - 0.0015, again, not significantly so) in the "pseudoword" condition.
> This does mean, however, that there is the chance the increase may differ
> between the "ideo" and "pseudoword" condition (which indeed is what
> your second analysis showed). In fact, if the standard errors are not too
> different over the conditions, taking the difference in the z-value between
> the two regression weights gives you a good first estimate for the difference
> between the two condition (in this case 0.8 - (-1.2) = 2), which indeed
> is close to the observed value.
>
> So, to sum things up, even with two non-significant regression weights
> for an interaction in a 3x2 design, you cannot be sure that there is
> no interaction, as the "middle" condition, which may be mapped on the intercept
> may not differ from the "high" and the "low" condition,

> Hi Holger,

> As I understand your question, you're looking for an LME analogue of an "omnibus" ANOVA analysis (one which would give you an F-test where the numerator has more than one degree of freedom). In this situation I would suggest using a likelihood ratio test between models with and without a fixed effect the critical factor (or interaction of factors, as appropriate).  As long as your dataset is reasonably large in comparison to the number of parameters in your models, the likelihood-ratio test should be only minimally anti-conservative (in the same way that t-statistics in LME models for psycholinguistic datasets are generally pretty close to normally distributed) its result will be invariant to the parametrization (i.e. the contrasts) you choose to represent your factors, and it will give
  you a result that you can interpret in much the same way as you would have interpreted an omnibus ANOVA's results.

I am finally back in town. When I read your email. I noticed that the chisq
for the interaction was 3.8. Note that this still allows for *one* of the

why it is anti-conservative.

Florian

>
> The thing is that the two regression weights for a 3x2 interaction (or the
> 3-level
> factor with a covariate) are something different from an F-test in an
> AN(c)OVA.
> The regression weights give you the differences for the "other" condition
> in
> comparison to the one mapped onto the intercept. This means that the two
> conditions not mapped onto the intercept are not compared to each other.
> An F test, however, takes into account the comparison of all conditions
> with each other.
>
> If you look at the two regression weights for the interaction in detail,
> it actually becomes obvious that a releveling may lead to a significant
> effect.
>
> The simple (NOT main) effect for centered trial is clearly significant
> which
> means that performance gets better in the "intensity" condition mapped on
> the intercept
> by 0.002261 per trial (as a side remark, it is easier to also normalize
> the range of the trial
> numbers to -0.5 to 0.5, so that the regression weights shows you directly
> how much things
> change over the course of the experiment).
>

> "ideo" condition

> "pseudoword" condition.

> between the "ideo" and "pseudoword" condition (which indeed is what
> your second analysis showed). In fact, if the standard errors are not too
> different over the conditions, taking the difference in the z-value between
> the two regression weights gives you a good first estimate for the
> difference
> between the two condition (in this case 0.8 - (-1.2) = 2), which indeed
> is close to the observed value.
>
> So, to sum things up, even with two non-significant regression weights

> no interaction, as the "middle" condition, which may be mapped on the
> intercept
> may not differ from the "high" and the "low" condition,
> while the latter two are significantly different.
>
> And here comes my question:
> Things actually get tricky when you have a three level factor. In most
> cases, it is possible to get around multiple testing issues by a clever
> choice of the intercept condition.
>
> What to do if not? Is there any accepted multiple mean comparison procedure
> for mixed-effect model (like Honest Significant Difference, of the
> Newman-Keuls
> procedure for an ANOVA)? Obviously, one can relevel and apply Bonferroni,
> but
> my understanding is that Bonferroni correction is a rather blunt
> instrument.

Hi Holger,

I agree with Roger, in principle all the information you need (the CIs)
should be derivable from one model fit. But let me ask another question:
why do you want to know what means are different from each other?
Presumably you have a hypothesis that you want to test -- when you ask this
question without a theory in mind, then these tests are post-hoc and should
be subject to multiple comparison corrections (e.g. using the multcomp)
package.

Florian

messages.subject: Re: Collinearity among predictors and interaction
messages.body_plain:
Dear Ariel,

I assume that your data is unbalanced with regard to A? i.e., the two
outcomes of A are not equally frequent? I they are, then I can only explain
the correlation if either B is correlated with A (though you're not
mentioning that) or if you're overfitting the data. Assuming it's the first
thing (your data is unbalanced with respect to A), consider recoding the A
to be

-2 * (n_posA/ n), if A == -1
2 * (n_negA / n), if A == 1


where n_posA is the number of data points for which A==1 and  n_negA is the
number of data points for which A==-1, n is the number of data points
(i.e., n = nA1 + nA0). I think this should remove the collinearity and the
interpretation should still be the one that you originally intended.
Hopefully, other folks have 2nd opinions.

Florian

Dear list,

I am analyzing a data set with two multi-level factors (4 and 5 levels)
varying over subjects and (partly) over items. As the data set is not
completely balanced and the dependent variable is yes/no,
I am using an lmer with a logistic linking function.

I ran into the problem of nonconvergence for the maximal model
if I include the interaction in the random effects
(which is not that suprising, because the number of random slopes
to be estimated for a 4x5 desgin is quite large). 

So I tried the following to get at least a glimpse at the possibility
of a significant interaction: I ran two models (one with and one
without the interaction) and only random intercepts for subject and item:

model1 = lmer(response ~ factor1*factor2 + (1|subject) + (1|item), ...)
model2 = lmer(response ~ factor1+factor2 + (1|subject) + (1|item), ...)
anova(model1,model2)

The model comparison is far from significant. As this is an anti-conservative
test, I should be in a safe position to assume that there is no interaction and
go on to test the "main" effects of these factors. 

Would the users of the list agree?

Kind regards,
Holger

messages.subject: Pearson chi-squared post hoc tests
messages.body_plain:
I've been using the chisqu.posthoc command in the polytomous package for
post hoc tests to Pearson chi-squared tests of independence.

http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/polytomous/polytomous.pdf

which gives three different post hoc test (following taken from the
manual):

X2.df the cellwise assessment

X2.df1 the cellwise assessment when df=1

std.pearson.residuals.sign the cellwise assessment of whether the absolute
value of a standardized Pearson residual is greater than
std.pearson.residual.min

Most of the time the post hoc tests match up but not always. What are the
main differences? More importantly, is one preferable?

Also, I was told that frequency counts can be misleading; look at the
residuals but I can find no explanation of why. I have one case in a tone
recognition study where tone 1 was misidentified as tone 3 far more than
tone was identified as any other tone but that cell is one of the ones
where the post hoc tests don't agree. The first one doesn't even have it as
contributing significantly. I was wondering where I could get a fuller
explanation of this.

Murray
